supporters.quote: Furthermore, older adults with depressive symptoms were highly associated with MCI (OR = 1.82, 95% CI = 1.20–2.76). (p.4) ... First, this study is based on a cross-sectional design. Thus, it is not possible to elucidate clear causal associations among sarcopenia, depressive symptoms, and cognitive function in older adults. (p.6)
supporters.note: Chen et al. 2021, J Affect Disord 286:71-77 (Tianjin and Shanghai community, N=1394, 241 MCI; cross-sectional). Supports only the narrower form: an adjusted cross-sectional association between depressive symptoms (GDS-30 >= 11) and MCI (memory complaint plus education-adjusted MMSE cut-off). It tests no direction. The ledger note's 'significant mediation running in both directions' is a misreading: the two mediation directions are between sarcopenia (and its components) and GDS score, with continuous MMSE score as the outcome, not depression-to-MCI versus MCI-to-depression. MCI is screen-defined (MMSE only).

supporters.quote: After full adjustment, baseline high-risk depressive symptoms were significantly associated with subsequent MCI (SHR = 1.20, 95%CI 1.08–1.34). Participants with baseline MCI are more likely to develop subsequent high-risk depressive symptoms than those without baseline MCI (SHR = 1.16, 95%CI 1.01–1.33). (p.1) ... Fourth, two separate models were run which are conceptually related to each other. ... While both show clear associations, it is difficult to determine bidirectionality without considering directional pathways in both directions in one model. (p.8)
supporters.note: Guo et al. 2023, J Affect Disord 338:449-458 (US Health and Retirement Study, 1998-2018, N=9317 and 9428; Fine-Gray competing-risks). The only supporter that tests both directions, and it finds both, at similar magnitude, in two separately fitted models; the authors themselves say bidirectionality cannot be determined this way and residual confounding cannot be ruled out, which bears equally on BOTH directions (same design, same data). It therefore supports 'reciprocally associated' as a longitudinal association in each direction, and it is the only basis for the clause that the reverse direction rests on a design that cannot separate reciprocity from a common cause. It gives little basis for 'the depression-to-MCI direction is better evidenced': the two SHRs overlap (1.20 vs 1.16); in the interaction models the MCI-to-depression main term lost significance (1.19, 0.97-1.45; 1.44, 0.96-2.17) while the depression-to-MCI term did not, but those are reference-category effects. Limits: MCI and dementia are defined from the HRS composite cognitive score (7-11), not clinically; depression is CES-D-8 >= 4; the excluded sample had more baseline exposure (healthier analytic cohort).

supporters.quote: Second, Fisher's exact test indicated that diagnosis of MDE was significantly associated with MCI (p = 0.027) and after multivariable adjustment for demographic and occupational covariates (adjusted RR = 1.64, 95 % CI = [1.20, 2.25], p = 0.002), as well as physical health covariates (adjusted RR = 1.62, 95 % CI = [1.16, 2.27], p = 0.005). ... After multivariable adjustment for demographics and occupation, diagnosis of MDE only was not significantly associated with MCI (p = 0.787). (p.5) ... First, the cross-sectional design precludes inferences about causality or the temporal sequence of PTSD, MDE, and MCI. (p.7)
supporters.note: Mann et al. 2026, Psychiatry Res 355:116827 (FDNY World Trade Center responders, N=337, 98.5% male, mean age 59.6; titled a cohort study but analysed cross-sectionally). Supports only a cross-sectional association of SCID-diagnosed major depressive episode with algorithmically defined MCI, and that association cannot be separated from PTSD: 12 of the 18 MDE cases had comorbid PTSD, MDE without PTSD (n=6) was not associated with MCI, and its population-attributable fraction was -0.3%. No direction is tested; the authors state they cannot tell whether depression precedes, follows or co-occurs with MCI. MCI prevalence of 45.4% in a working-age firefighter cohort reflects a broad algorithmic definition. Generalisability is limited to a trauma-exposed, almost entirely male occupational group.

supporters.quote: Using a random-effects model, the pooled prevalence of StD among older adults with MCI was estimated at 28.1 % (95 % CI: 24.2 %−32.0 %). Substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies (I2 = 98.4 %, τ2 = 0.019, p < 0.001) (see Fig. 2).
supporters.note: Huang et al. 2026, Psychiatry Res 357:116922 (52 studies, 29,321 older adults with MCI). Searched for a comparison with cognitively unimpaired older adults, a relative measure, or any directional analysis: there is none. It is a single-arm prevalence of subthreshold depression (MDD explicitly excluded where assessed) within MCI; its only comparisons are with prevalence figures for depression in MCI and dementia from other reviews. A prevalence without a non-MCI reference does not establish an association, let alone a reciprocal one; its statements about depression driving progression are citations of other studies (Lee 2012; Rosenberg 2013). Egger's test suggested publication bias (p = 0.040), although trim-and-fill imputed no studies; I2 = 98.4%, and 46 of 52 studies ascertained 'StD' without a clinical assessment for MDD.

supporters.quote: Articles were included if longitudinal (i.e., to appropriately assess risk of progression), assessed MCI at baseline using the criteria outlined above and AD-type dementia at follow-up, and reported on risk factors for progression of MCI to AD. (p.4) ... It is unclear whether the relationship between depressive symptoms and AD is because depression is a prodrome of AD, depression is a risk factor for AD, a third variable causes both conditions, or some combination of these hypotheses. (p.13)
supporters.note: Meynadasy et al. 2025, AJGP Open Sci Educ Pract 8:17-32 (systematic review of 17 longitudinal human studies plus a narrative rodent section). Every included study starts from MCI and asks about progression to AD, so the review addresses depression as a prognostic factor WITHIN MCI, not the association between depressive symptomatology and MCI, and not either direction of that association. It reports only other studies' results, several of them null or contrary (depression without apathy not associated with conversion in NACC; history of depression not associated in ADNI; no converter difference on GDS in J-ADNI; depression polygenic score not associated). By the ledger's own reasoning for dropping P-647 ('evidence about prognosis rather than about the association ... belongs with VF-27'), this paper does not belong in VF-26 either.

narrowed_wording: Depressive symptoms (or major depression) and MCI are associated in three independent samples of different design: longitudinally in the US Health and Retirement Study (P-646), and cross-sectionally in a Chinese community sample (P-644) and in World Trade Center responders, where the association could not be separated from comorbid PTSD (P-656). Direction was tested in only one study, which found both directions at similar magnitude in two separately fitted models that cannot separate reciprocal causation from a shared common cause; the reviewed studies therefore establish neither reciprocity nor that the depression-to-MCI direction is better evidenced.
reasoning: As the Table A1 row states it, the convergence makes three claims: a reciprocal association, a better-evidenced depression-to-MCI direction, and a design-limited reverse direction. Only P-646 answers yes: it is the only supporter that tests direction, and it finds both directions (SHR 1.20 and 1.16) in separately fitted competing-risks models whose authors concede they cannot establish bidirectionality. P-644 and P-656 support only a cross-sectional association and test no direction; P-656's depression effect is carried by comorbid PTSD (depression without PTSD, six responders, not associated). P-657 is a prevalence of subthreshold depression within MCI with no non-MCI reference, so it supports no association. P-912 is a review of depression as a predictor of MCI-to-Alzheimer's progression, a prognostic question the ledger itself assigns to VF-27 when it drops P-647. So fewer than three supporters sustain the reciprocal form. The 'depression-to-MCI is better evidenced' clause has no support beyond P-646, where both directions share one design and have overlapping estimates; cross-sectional studies that model depression as the exposure are not evidence of direction. The narrower claim of an association does hold: P-646, P-644 and P-656 give three independent datasets (HRS, Tianjin/Shanghai community, FDNY) and three method families (competing-risks survival, logistic regression, robust quasi-Poisson), with one of the three unable to separate depression from PTSD. This matches the association-only wording the review already uses in Section 4.5 ('robustly associated ... with both directions tested in only one of these studies'), but not the Table A1 row. The record's claim of five dataset and five method families is not borne out, since two of its five supporters do not bear on the association. The dichotomisation caveat stands (P-646 used continuous scores only in a sensitivity model; P-656's dimensional analysis used a combined PTSD-and-depression symptom count).
